locator.heading: Alexander

source_text:
IT is called Alisander, Horse-parsley, and Wild-parsley, and the Black
Pot-herb; the seed of it is that which is usually sold in apothecaries’
shops for Macedonian Parsley-seed.

_Descript._] It is usually sown in all the gardens in Europe, and so
well known, that it needs no farther description.

_Time._] It flowers in June and July; the seed is ripe in August.

_Government and virtues._] It is an herb of Jupiter, and therefore
friendly to nature, for it warms a cold stomach, and opens a stoppage
of the liver and spleen; it is good to move women’s courses, to
expel the afterbirth, to break wind, to provoke urine, and helps the
stranguary; and these things the seeds will do likewise. If either of
them be boiled in wine, or being bruised and taken in wine, is also
effectual against the biting of serpents. And you know what Alexander
pottage is good for, that you may no longer eat it out of ignorance but
out of knowledge.

evidence.summary: Modern literature supports parsley's traditional use as a diuretic for urinary retention and digestive aid. Evidence regarding uterine effects (amenorrhea) or specific organ stoppage is less robust, often relying on historical context rather than clinical trials.

No modern scientific evidence or reviews were found for Conopodium majus regarding its traditional uses for cold stomach, retained afterbirth, or organ stoppage. The lack of recent literature suggests these applications remain unverified by contemporary pharmacological standards.

concordance.rationale: Modern reviews (PMID: 38189231) confirm diuretic effects for urinary retention but lack clinical evidence for other claims like liver stoppage or serpent bites.
concordance.uncertainty: High uncertainty due to absence of modern clinical trials for most historical indications.
caveats: Claims are based on traditional use and pharmacological plausibility only.
No evidence supports efficacy for venomous bites or reproductive regulation.
